title: Learning and Encounters in the Seaside City of Gdansk
paragraphs: I did a three-month clinical clerkship at the Medical University of Gdansk in Poland. Gdansk is a port town in northern Poland, and although its name recognition in Japan is low, it is a wonderful city that tourists from all over Europe visit for its beautiful old town and beaches. The Medical University of Gdansk, located in such a city, is one of Poland's leading medical education institutions.

We took part in the English Division of the Medical University of Gdansk and did clinical clerkships together with students from various backgrounds. I chose obstetrics and gynecology, neurosurgery, transplant surgery, emergency medicine, dermatology, gastroenterology, nephrology and surgery. The doctors gave lectures in fluent English rather than Polish, so I was not left behind because of the language barrier, and there were equal opportunities to speak. Since many patients could speak English, I was also allowed to take histories and physical findings, and I could have a fulfilling clerkship. What impressed me most through the clerkship was the difference between European and Japanese medical education. For example, when they memorize treatments, they are required to memorize not only the types of drugs and methods of administration but also trade names and doses properly. It is also hard to graduate from medical school straight through, reportedly taking eight years on average. In addition, to enter the department one wishes, good grades and achievements in papers are needed, so students aspiring to highly competitive departments made more effort than their classmates.

The Medical University of Gdansk prepared a dormitory for us. The shower, toilet and kitchen were shared, and the dormitory was surrounded by wild animals such as wild boars, but I got used to it after a while and lived there, grateful to be accepted. Eating out is more expensive than in Japan, so apart from when I went out with friends I basically cooked for myself. Polish is completely different from English and hard to guess, so I worked hard at buying food each time, taking my time.

The main reasons I applied to the Medical University of Gdansk were that I could do the clerkship in English and that there were rich opportunities to interact with students. Because I did the clerkship together with them, I naturally warmed to them. As mentioned above, students gather in the English Division from all over the world, including exchange students. Besides the major countries of Europe, I made friends of truly diverse nationalities, with students from Slovenia, Slovakia and Bulgaria, and from Nigeria, Iran, Sri Lanka, Laos and so on. With the students I became close to, I went out on holidays, cooked together and even met at travel destinations, and made many memories. On the day of parting, we all felt reluctant to leave and savored the good fortune of having met. Having spent the special time of studying abroad together, firm bonds were formed, and I am convinced that however many years away the next time we meet may be, we will be able to spend time happily again just the same.

I had hoped to take part in this program since entering university and had polished both practical English and medical English in my own way. I feel that, including the difficulties and incidents, I was able to live the fulfilling life abroad that I had hoped for. I am convinced that the adaptability, communication skills and understanding of other cultures cultivated in this experience will certainly be of use in the future. I express my gratitude to Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川, Dr. Itzel and all the members of the International Collaboration Office, who made efforts to carry out this study abroad, and to everyone who looked after me locally.
